correctness.rationale: Non-cut-vertex deletion and exact graph isomorphism give a complete class census; independent dominating sets and rational first-choice recursion give the two laws exactly. The check compares adjacent ratios on common size support for all 2,571 graph classes; adjacency of support points suffices by transitivity. The quantitative theorem and finite verification are unchanged.
residual_risks: The priority-permutation checks share the census generator and extend only through order six. The exact likelihood-ratio conclusion extends only through order ten and only for the connected class.

evidence: The paper reports first-order stochastic dominance on all connected subcubic graphs through order twelve (27,525 classes).
broader_coverage.reasoning: The paper covers a larger vertex-order range, but a weaker order relation. The printed claim does not imply the finite likelihood-ratio theorem.

evidence: First-order dominance compares cumulative probabilities, whereas likelihood-ratio order compares every ordered pair of point probabilities. The probability vectors (1/3,1/3,1/3) and (1/6,1/2,1/3) demonstrate that first-order dominance does not imply likelihood-ratio order. The related six-vertex counterexample is excluded by the subcubic hypothesis.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The exact ratios require a stronger check on the stated domain, not a restatement of first-order coverage. The content of code not reported in the paper remains a separate priority question.

evidence: Random priorities give the same greedy size distribution, and a uniformly chosen independent dominating set gives the static size law. The related exact six-vertex failure is outside the degree cap.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The equivalent statement must concern the ratios of size probabilities. Inequalities or uniformity for individual configurations are not equivalent to comparing aggregated sizes.

value.rationale: The strengthened comparison on a naturally motivated sparse graph class tests the full occupancy-size laws, not just FOSD or graph-class counts. The unrestricted-degree six-vertex obstruction gives a concrete reason to check this stronger property separately. The finite equality count characterizes when the laws are genuinely separated at order ten.
